title: Ramayana's Rs 1,600 Crore Gamble: Inside Bollywood's Most Expensive Film Ever
excerpt: Ranbir Kapoor's two-part epic, backed by Hans Zimmer's score and DNEG's Oscar-winning VFX, aims for a Diwali 2026 release as Sunny Deol calls playing Hanuman 'not easy.'
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Ramayana's ₹1,600 crore budget makes it India's most expensive film franchise ever.
  • Part 1 releases on November 6, 2026; Part 2 follows in 2027.
  • Sunny Deol calls playing Hanuman a challenging role, promising to do justice.
  • Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman collaborate on the film's score.
  • Ramayana needs ₹9,600 crore to match profit ratios of earlier films.

Required Earnings to Break Even
  • Ramayana's combined two-part budget of ₹1,600 crore makes it the most expensive Indian film franchise ever, dwarfing Baahubali 2 (₹250 crore) and RRR (₹550 crore).
  • Part 1 releases Diwali 2026 (November 6), Part 2 on Diwali 2027. The trailer premieres globally at San Diego Comic-Con on July 24.
  • Sunny Deol, who plays Lord Hanuman, told reporters the role was “not easy” and promised to do justice to the character.
  • Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman are collaborating on the score; DNEG (Dune, Interstellar) handles VFX.

The numbers behind Bollywood’s Ramayana are staggering. With a combined budget of ₹1,600 crore across two parts, the Nitesh Tiwari-directed epic is the most expensive Indian film ever made — more than three times the cost of RRR and six times what Baahubali 2 cost to produce.

Part 1 of the film, starring Ranbir Kapoor as Lord Ram, Yash as Ravana, and Sai Pallavi as Sita, is set for a Diwali 2026 release on November 6. Part 2 follows on Diwali 2027, with producers planning to leverage existing sets and VFX assets to bring the second installment in at ₹700 crore.

Sunny Deol on Playing Hanuman

Sunny Deol, cast as Lord Hanuman, told reporters this week that the role was “not easy” and promised to give his best to the character. The veteran actor acknowledged the weight of playing one of Hinduism’s most revered figures, saying he felt a deep responsibility to do justice to the role.

At a separate event in Delhi where the trailer was screened for a select audience, Yash praised his co-star’s commitment to the project.

“Ranbir Kapoor has been phenomenal. I think the whole of India will understand how deeply he has surrendered to this role and see the magic he has created.”

— Yash, who plays Ravana in Ramayana

Global Ambitions

The film’s marketing strategy signals ambitions far beyond the Indian market. The first full trailer will premiere at San Diego Comic-Con’s Ballroom 20 on July 24 — a venue historically reserved for the biggest reveals from major Hollywood studios. It will then be screened across thousands of Indian theaters in multiple languages, including 3D and IMAX formats.

The production reflects that global reach. Hans Zimmer, who scored The Dark Knight and Dune, is collaborating with A.R. Rahman on the music — a fusion of Western orchestral scale and Indian soul. DNEG, the Oscar-winning visual effects studio behind Interstellar and Blade Runner 2049, is handling the film’s VFX.

The Box Office Math

The economics are daunting. According to Koimoi’s analysis, Ramayana would need to earn approximately ₹9,600 crore to match the profit ratio of the first Bollywood film on Lord Ram, adjusting for inflation and the vastly higher production costs. That figure underscores the gamble: even if the film becomes the highest-grossing Indian movie ever, the margins on a ₹1,600 crore investment remain razor-thin.

For context, Ranveer Singh’s Dhurandhar 2, currently the highest-grossing Indian film worldwide without China, earned around ₹1,800 crore. Ramayana would need to nearly match that figure just to break even on Part 1 alone.

A Star-Studded Cast

The supporting cast adds further depth to the production. Veteran actor Arun Govil, who played Ram in the iconic 1987 television series, returns as King Dasharath. Rakul Preet Singh plays Shurpanakha, Kajal Aggarwal is Mandodari, Ravi Dubey plays Lakshman, and Raghav Juyal takes on the role of Meghanad.

Producer Namit Malhotra of Prime Focus Studios views the combined budget as a single investment in the franchise. His VFX company DNEG has been tasked with creating hyper-realistic depictions of Ayodhya, Lanka, and Hanuman’s aerial feats — settings that require the kind of technical sophistication typically seen in Hollywood’s biggest blockbusters.

Whether this ₹1,600 crore bet pays off will become clear during the Diwali box office battle. For the Indian diaspora, the July 24 Comic-Con premiere offers the first real glimpse of whether Bollywood’s most ambitious project lives up to its price tag.
